notes.b: Fresh meat spoils quickly and the cheaper cuts can be tough. Processing changes meat from its fresh state, usually to make it convenient, to make it keep longer, or to put cheaper cuts and trimmings to use.
points: Processed meat is meat that has been minced, salted, cured, smoked, cooked, canned, frozen or otherwise altered before sale, for example by adding other ingredients.

Examples include frozen burgers, nuggets and sausages; black and white pudding; rashers, bacon, gammon and cooked ham; luncheon meat, cold cuts and salami; canned stew and corned beef; dehydrated or freeze-dried meat in soups and meals; and ready meals and pies.
Cured meats such as bacon and ham contain salt and curing salts (sodium nitrite), which give them a pink colour and a cured flavour.
Minced products are made from trimmings (small pieces cut off when the carcass is prepared), offal and fat, with seasonings and binders added, so little of the carcass is wasted.
Textured vegetable protein (TVP), a dried soya product, is used as a meat extender, meaning it replaces some of the meat in burgers and stews and makes the product cheaper.

Typical ingredients are minced meat, fat, water, salt, herbs and spices, rusk or breadcrumbs as a binder (to hold the mixture together), and additives such as preservatives (nitrite), colours, flavour enhancers and antioxidants.
Food additives in processed meat must be approved under Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives, and products list them by E number.

On the label, ingredients are listed in descending order of weight, the meat content is declared where the name stresses meat, and allergens such as cereals containing gluten, soya, mustard and celery are emphasised.
notes.tip: If asked for two types of processed meat, name them (for example burgers, sausages, bacon, ham, cooked meats, canned corned beef or dehydrated TVP products) and give one advantage of each, such as economy, little waste, convenience, long shelf life, speed of cooking or variety. TVP as an extender is dried soya protein replacing some meat.

notes.h: Advantages and disadvantages of processed meat
notes.b: Processed meat is popular because it is cheap, quick and keeps well, but the same processing adds salt, fat and additives. When asked to evaluate it, weigh the benefits against the health drawbacks.
points: Economy: products are cheap per portion because they can use cheaper cuts and trimmings.
Little waste: all parts of the carcass are used, and portions are uniform in size.
Convenience: products cook quickly and need little preparation, cooking skill or equipment.
Fuel and labour saving: a frozen product often needs only reheating, so less fuel and time are used.
Long shelf life: frozen, canned and cured products keep far longer than fresh meat, and some canned or dried products can be stored for months without refrigeration.
Variety: different flavours, shapes and sizes give choice and appeal to children.

Disadvantages: high salt content can contribute to high blood pressure, and many products are high in saturated fat from fatty trimmings. Health advice is to limit processed meat for its salt, saturated fat and bowel-cancer risk.

Many products contain added water, fillers and additives, so their meat content is lower than the name suggests and their nutritional quality is lower than fresh lean meat. Freezing retains most nutrients, while canning and dehydration lose some B vitamins.
notes.tip: When asked to evaluate, give both sides: advantages such as cost, convenience, shelf life and use of less tender cuts, against disadvantages such as salt, saturated fat, additives and lower meat content. A processed meat is not unhealthy for every nutrient, so avoid one-sided answers.

notes.b: Every process that extends the shelf life of meat works by blocking one of the causes of spoilage, so it helps to know what those causes are.
points: Meat spoils through micro-organisms (bacteria and moulds), the meat's own enzymes, oxidation of fat (which causes rancidity, an unpleasant stale taste) and drying.
Bacteria need moisture, warmth, air, nutrients and time to grow, so each preservation process removes or controls one of these.
notes.tip: Write the principle as its own sentence for any process: low temperature, removal of air, osmosis, high heat or removal of water. Do not mix these up.

notes.h: Processes that extend the shelf life of meat
notes.b: Different processes use cold, lack of air, salt, smoke, heat or dryness to slow or stop spoilage. Extending shelf life means slowing spoilage, not sterilising the meat, except in canning.
points: Refrigeration (5 °C or below): keeping meat chilled slows bacterial growth and enzyme activity, extending its life by days, but it does not kill bacteria, so meat should be covered or wrapped.
Listeria monocytogenes can still grow at refrigerator temperatures, so ready-to-eat cooked and cured meats need careful hygiene and use-by dates.
Freezing: low temperatures stop microbial growth and enzyme activity, so frozen meat keeps for months.

Vacuum packing: air is removed and the meat sealed in strong plastic, so aerobic micro-organisms (those that need oxygen) cannot grow. The pack is not sterile, so it must be kept refrigerated, carries a use-by date and is treated as fresh meat once opened.

Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP): air in a sealed tray is replaced with a gas mix, usually carbon dioxide, which inhibits aerobic bacteria, and nitrogen, an inert gas that stops the pack collapsing. Oxygen is used for fresh red meat to keep its colour. It needs refrigeration and a use-by date.
Curing and salting: salt, sugar and nitrite draw water from micro-organisms and inhibit spoilage bacteria.

Smoking: after curing, the meat is hung in smoke from burning hardwood sawdust. Smoke compounds (which are antibacterial and antioxidant) and light drying of the surface slow microbial growth and add flavour, and smoking is usually combined with curing.

Canning: meat is prepared, cooked and sealed in cans, then heated to a high temperature under pressure (heat-sterilised), destroying micro-organisms and inactivating enzymes. The airtight seal stops microbes re-entering, so cans keep for years at room temperature.

Dehydration: removing moisture stops microbes growing, since they need water to multiply. Freeze-drying removes water from frozen meat under vacuum. Dried meat is light and long-lasting and is rehydrated in dishes such as soups and ready meals.
notes.tip: For a full answer on one process, write its name, how it is carried out, the underlying principle and its effect on meat (colour, texture, flavour, nutrients) with product examples. A list of several processes does not earn full marks. Link vacuum or MAP packing to the need for refrigeration and a use-by date. Salt does not poison microbes; it dehydrates them by osmosis, and nitrite is the key to pink colour and botulism control.

notes.b: Curing is a good process to know in full because it covers the three parts examiners ask for: how it is done, why it works and what it does to the meat.
points: Method: meat is cooled and trimmed, then rubbed with salt and curing salts, or injected with or soaked in brine containing salt, sugar and curing salts (sodium nitrite), and held in a cool room for several days.
Method: after curing, the meat may be smoked, or sold green (unsmoked and uncooked) as raw cured meat.
Principle: salt draws water out of micro-organisms by osmosis, dehydrating them and reducing the water available for growth.
Principle: nitrite inhibits spoilage bacteria, including Clostridium botulinum (the bacterium that causes botulism), and fixes the pink colour of cured meat.
Effect on meat: there is little loss of nutritive value, but the sodium content rises because of the salt added.
Effect on meat: the meat becomes firmer and drier, and its flavour changes to a salty, cured taste.
Examples of cured products are bacon, rashers, gammon and cooked ham.
Diagram: a flow diagram of curing, from cooled meat to brine or dry salt, a cold room for several days, then smoked or sold green.
notes.tip: Say 'several days' for the time in the cold room, not a set number. Do not use specific curing times.

notes.b: Freezing is the cheapest way, along with refrigeration, to keep meat for months. It works by cold rather than by chemicals or heat.
points: Method: meat is boned, trimmed and portioned, wrapped in moisture-proof packaging, then blast frozen (frozen very fast at about -30 °C) and stored at -18 °C or below.
Principle: low temperatures inhibit enzyme activity and microbial growth, and the water in the meat turns to ice, which is unavailable to micro-organisms.
Principle: fast freezing gives small ice crystals that damage the meat's cells less, and wrapping keeps out microbes and prevents freezer burn.

Effect on meat: colour, flavour, texture and most nutrients are retained, although slight losses of extractives (flavour compounds), B vitamins and minerals occur in drip (the liquid lost on thawing).
Effect on meat: freezer burn (dry, pale patches) and rancidity occur if the packaging fails and the meat is exposed to air.
Diagram: a flow diagram of freezing, from boning and trimming to wrapping, blast freezing and storage.
notes.tip: Mention small ice crystals from fast freezing and the effect on nutrients and texture, as well as the principle of low temperature.

notes.h: Canning and dehydration: effect on meat
notes.b: Canning and dehydration change meat more than chilling or freezing does, which is why their effects on nutrients and texture are worth stating.
points: Canning: meat is prepared and cooked, packed in cans with brine, sauce or liquid, air is removed, and the cans are sealed and heat-sterilised under pressure.
Canned meat has a shelf life of years at room temperature, and the meat is tender and cooked.
Canning causes a loss of B vitamins, especially thiamine, and changes texture and flavour.
Dehydration and freeze-drying: water is removed using hot air, or by freeze-drying under vacuum, and micro-organisms cannot grow without water.
Dehydrated meat is light and long-lasting, but there is some loss of B vitamins and a change in texture, as in the dried meat found in soups and ready meals.
notes.tip: Canning uses heat, dehydration removes water, freezing uses cold and curing uses salt. Do not confuse these principles.

keyTerms.definition: Meat that has been minced, salted, cured, smoked, cooked or otherwise altered before sale.
Preserving meat by adding salt, sugar and curing salts so that micro-organisms are inhibited.
The movement of water across a membrane from a weaker to a stronger salt solution, which dehydrates micro-organisms in salted meat.
A curing salt that inhibits spoilage bacteria and gives cured meat its pink colour.
Packaging meat after air has been removed, which prevents aerobic micro-organisms from growing.
Packaging in which the air is replaced with a gas mixture that slows the spoilage of meat.
Sealing food in cans and heat-sterilising it, which destroys micro-organisms and inactivates enzymes.
A dried soya protein product that is rehydrated and used to extend meat in some products.
Freezing meat quickly in a very cold air blast so that it freezes rapidly.

questions.prompt: Give two examples of processed meat products and explain one reason why consumers buy them.
questions.model: Two examples, one mark each: sausages, rashers, cooked ham, burgers, nuggets, salami, canned corned beef. One reason, with explanation for full marks: convenience, because they cook quickly with little preparation; economy, because they are cheap per portion and use cheaper cuts and trimmings; long shelf life, so they can be stored in the freezer or pantry.

questions.prompt: Describe one process used to extend the shelf life of meat, referring to the method, the principle behind it and its effect on the meat.
questions.model: Freezing: method, meat boned, trimmed and wrapped in moisture-proof packaging, then blast frozen. Principle: low temperatures inhibit enzyme activity and microbial growth; moisture turns to ice, which is unavailable to micro-organisms. Effect on the meat: colour, texture and most nutrients retained; slight loss of B vitamins and minerals in drip; freezer burn if packaging fails; the meat keeps for months. Alternative accepted: curing, with method of brine or dry cure and holding in a cool room; principle of osmosis drawing water from micro-organisms and nitrite inhibiting spoilage bacteria; effect of a rise in sodium, firmer and drier texture and a pink colour.
